badges.years: Approx. 2008-2023 (colored crest on silver cap; exact years can't be confirmed from the front)
badges.description: This shiny round cap sat in the middle of a Porsche wheel and spun around super fast! It shows the famous Porsche crest, a golden shield with red and black stripes, spiky black antlers, and a black horse rearing up on its back legs in the very center.
badges.fun_fact: The black horse comes from the coat of arms of Stuttgart, the German city where Porsche builds its cars. The city's name comes from an old word for a horse farm!

badges.description: This shiny metal badge comes from the back of a classic Audi 100 LS, a comfy family sedan from the early 1970s! The big '100 LS' sits on a long silver line, and the fancy curly word 'Automatic' underneath told everyone the car could shift gears all by itself. The little bumps and spots show it has been on a real adventure for about 50 years!
badges.fun_fact: The Audi 100 was the car that brought the Audi name back to life after World War II. It sold so well that it helped Audi grow into the big car company it is today.

badges.description: This shiny chrome mustang horse is galloping at full speed right through a giant Roman numeral 'II'! It stood up proudly on the hood of the Ford Mustang II, a smaller and lighter Mustang built in the 1970s. Look closely and you can see the horse's flowing tail, pointy ears, and legs stretched out mid-run!
badges.fun_fact: The Mustang II came out in 1974, during a gas shortage. Ford made it smaller to save fuel, and it sold over 385,000 cars in its very first year!

badges.description: This shiny badge shows Opel's famous lightning bolt zooming right through a silver circle, like a flash of power! The bolt pokes out both sides of the ring, so it looks like it's racing through. Cars like the Opel Astra, Corsa and Vectra wore this badge on their noses and tails.
badges.fun_fact: Opel's lightning bolt comes from a fast Opel truck called the 'Blitz', which is the German word for lightning!

badges.description: This shiny oval shows a bright red trident, the three-pointed spear held by Neptune, the Roman god of the sea! Below it, a deep blue stripe spells out MASERATI in silver letters. Badges like this one went on fast, fancy Italian sports cars.
badges.fun_fact: The Maserati trident was inspired by the statue of Neptune in a fountain in Bologna, Italy, where Maserati was founded in 1914.

badges.description: This shiny chrome badge rode on the front of the hood of an old Ford pickup truck. It shows a big gear, like the ones that turn inside machines, with a zigzag lightning bolt zapping right through it, all on a red striped background. Five stars sit on top like a row of medals!
badges.fun_fact: Ford used the gear and lightning bolt as a symbol for its trucks to show power and hard work: the gear stands for strong machinery and the lightning bolt stands for energy and speed.

badges.description: This shiny badge comes from a Lada, a tough little car built in the Soviet Union, now Russia. The chrome shape is a Viking-style sailboat called a 'ladya', and its sail also makes the Russian letter 'В' for VAZ, the factory that built it. It sits on a bright orange-red background like a sail on a sunset sea!
badges.fun_fact: The first Lada, the VAZ-2101, was based on the Italian Fiat 124, and millions were built. Some are still driving around today, more than 50 years later!

badges.description: This tough black center cap comes from a Raceline wheel, the kind often put on trucks, Jeeps and off-road machines. A big shiny silver 'R' sits in the middle like a racing flag, with the word RACELINE spinning around it twice between little stars. Real metal bolts held it tight to the wheel so it wouldn't fly off on bumpy trails!
badges.fun_fact: Raceline is known for making beadlock wheels, which clamp the tire onto the wheel so it stays on even when off-roaders let air out of their tires for extra grip on rocks and sand.

badges.years: Approx. 1975-1990 (best guess from the wreath-and-crest style)
badges.description: This shiny chrome badge has a fancy laurel wreath wrapped around it, like the leaf crowns that champions won long ago! In the middle is a bold triangle with gold and red colors, and at the bottom are letters that look like 'SE', which probably told people this was a special fancier version of the car. Its black sparkly background makes the chrome really pop!
badges.fun_fact: Laurel wreaths have been a sign of winning since ancient Greece, where champions at the Olympic-style games wore crowns of leaves. That's why carmakers put wreaths on their fancy trim badges!

badges.description: This shiny round badge shows Harley-Davidson's famous 'Number One' logo, but with a sneaky twist: the top of the big '1' is shaped like a skull with two spooky eyes! It comes from the world of Harley motorcycles, where riders bolt cool round covers and caps like this onto their bikes.
badges.fun_fact: Harley-Davidson was started in 1903 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, by William Harley and the Davidson brothers. Their very first motorcycles were built in a small wooden shed!

badges.description: This is the famous Land Rover oval, painted deep green with shiny gold letters that look like real treasure! The slanted words LAND ROVER have little arrow tips that make them look like they are zooming forward. A badge like this rode on tough British off-road trucks that climb mountains and splash through rivers.
badges.fun_fact: The very first Land Rover from 1948 was sketched in the sand on a beach in Wales, and early Land Rovers were painted leftover green airplane paint after World War II!

badges.description: This shiny silver badge says 'SERIES II' in big, fast-looking slanted letters. A giant Roman numeral 'II' zooms behind the word, with lightning-bolt lines that make it look like it's racing! Car makers used 'Series II' to show that a model was the second, improved version.
badges.fun_fact: 'II' is the Roman numeral for 2. Car makers often use Roman numerals on badges because they look fancy and important, like the numbers on an old clock!

badges.description: This shiny badge shows the 'Growler,' a jaguar's face with its mouth wide open, roaring and showing its sharp teeth! The word JAGUAR wraps around the top of the chrome ring, and the dark greenish background makes the silver big cat pop out like it's ready to pounce.
badges.fun_fact: Jaguar has two famous cat logos: the 'Leaper,' a jaguar jumping forward, and the 'Growler,' the roaring face on this badge, which often appears on the wheels and grille!

badges.description: This shiny badge shows the famous MINI wings! A round circle with the word MINI sits in the middle, and chrome wings stretch out on both sides like the car is ready to fly. It comes from the modern MINI Cooper era, when this puffy 3D chrome logo was used.
badges.fun_fact: The original Mini from 1959 was so small and clever that about 80% of the car's floor space was for people and luggage, and the modern MINI brand is now owned by BMW!

badges.badge_name: Rear Boot Lid 'E TYPE' Script Badge
badges.description: This shiny chrome badge spells out 'E TYPE', and the giant 'E' stretches its bottom like a speedy racing stripe under the other letters! It came from the back of the Jaguar E-Type, a super-sleek British sports car with a hood so long it looks like a rocket on wheels.
badges.fun_fact: The Jaguar E-Type is so beautiful that a real one is kept at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, just like a famous painting!

badges.description: This shiny silver badge spells out SAAB in bold, chunky letters that look like they were carved from metal! The two pointy A's have little triangle windows, and the brushed silver shines when you tilt it in the light. Badges like this were worn by Saab cars from Sweden.
badges.fun_fact: Saab started out building airplanes, not cars! The name comes from Svenska Aeroplan Aktiebolaget, which means Swedish Aeroplane Company.

badges.description: This shiny blue badge shows a fierce red griffin, a make-believe creature that is half eagle and half lion, wearing a golden king's crown! Under the griffin, silver letters spell SAAB, the name of a car company from Sweden. Badges like this were on the front, back or wheels of Saab cars.
badges.fun_fact: Saab started out building airplanes, and the company still makes fighter jets in Sweden today, even though it stopped making cars around 2011!

badges.badge_name: Dog Dish Hubcap / Wheel Center Cap
badges.description: This shiny silver hubcap has the famous Chevy bowtie right in the middle, sitting on a cool blue shield like a superhero badge. The three pointy ribs make it look like it's spinning even when it's standing still! It probably covered the wheel of an old Chevy pickup truck from your grandparents' time.
badges.fun_fact: Collectors call small hubcaps like this 'dog dish' hubcaps because they look like a little bowl you could feed a dog from!

badges.description: This shiny badge spells out VOLVO in big silver letters, with a special shield on the end that says 144. Under the number is a bright red patch with a big chrome S, which told everyone this was the sporty 'S' version with a stronger engine! It came off a boxy Swedish family car built about 55 years ago.
badges.fun_fact: Volvo's '144' name was a code: 1 meant the 100 series, the first 4 meant four cylinders, and the last 4 meant four doors!

badges.description: This shiny blue badge shows a fierce red griffin, a mythical creature with an eagle's head and a lion's body, wearing a golden royal crown! It came from a Saab, a car from Sweden built by a company that also made jet airplanes and huge Scania trucks. That's why the badge says both SAAB and SCANIA.
badges.fun_fact: The crowned griffin comes from the coat of arms of Skåne, a region in southern Sweden that is called Scania in English. Saab also built fighter jets, so the cars had airplane-inspired designs!

badges.description: This is a Volvo wheel center cap that sat right in the middle of a car's wheel, spinning around as the car drove! It shows a shiny chrome circle with an arrow shooting out from the top corner, and a black bar across the middle that says VOLVO in silver letters. This modern 3D chrome version of the logo arrived around 2015, starting with the second-generation XC90 SUV.
badges.fun_fact: The circle-and-arrow on Volvo's logo is an ancient symbol for iron, chosen to show how strong Swedish steel is, and the name 'Volvo' means 'I roll' in Latin, which is perfect for a wheel cap!

badges.description: This is the famous Jaguar 'Leaper', a shiny chrome jaguar caught in mid-pounce! It sat right on the front of the hood, so the jaguar looked like it was racing ahead of the car. Look closely and you can see its stretched-out paws, its long, strong body and its curly tail.
badges.fun_fact: Many countries later banned pointy hood ornaments for safety, so Jaguar made a spring-loaded Leaper that folds down if bumped. Later cars dropped it and used a flat 'growler' badge showing the jaguar's face instead.

badges.description: This shiny badge shows a mighty trident, the magic three-pointed spear of Neptune, the king of the sea! It sits inside a five-sided pentagon shape, a nod to Chrysler's famous Pentastar logo. The trident is Maserati's sign, so the badge mixes an American car company with an Italian sports car company.
badges.fun_fact: Maserati's trident logo comes from the statue of Neptune in a fountain in Bologna, Italy, the city where the Maserati brothers started their company.

badges.description: This shiny chrome badge shows Nissan's famous logo: a bold bar with the name NISSAN stretched across a circle, like a sign in front of a rising sun. The circle is filled with sparkly silver paint that glitters in the light. It would have sat proudly on the front or back of a Nissan car or truck from the 1990s!
badges.fun_fact: Nissan's circle-and-bar logo comes from an older design called Datsun. Nissan cars sold in America were called Datsuns until the early 1980s!

badges.years: approx. 1985-2009 (sharp chrome chevron style, before the rounded 2009 logo)
badges.description: These two shiny chrome arrows are the famous Citroën 'double chevron' logo from France! When they're on the car they point straight up like two rockets. The sharp ridge down the middle makes them sparkle in the sunlight.
badges.fun_fact: Citroën's founder, André Citroën, got the double chevron idea from gears whose teeth were shaped like V's. His company made those gears before it ever built a car!

badges.badge_name: Double Chevron Emblem (pair of chrome chevrons)
badges.description: These two shiny chrome arrows are the famous 'double chevron' logo of Citroën, the French carmaker! Turn them so the points face up and you'll see the badge just like it sits on the car. Their thin, pointy shape looks like the older style used before Citroën switched to bigger, rounder chevrons.
badges.fun_fact: Citroën's two chevrons come from gears! Founder André Citroën started out making gears with V-shaped teeth, so he used that zig-zag gear tooth shape as his car logo.

badges.years: Approx. 2000-2016 (separate chrome 3D chevrons; exact model can't be confirmed from the front)
badges.description: These two shiny chrome arrows are the famous Citroën 'double chevron' badge! Turn them so they point up and you'll see the logo French Citroën cars wear on their noses and tails. Their sharp, pointy shape makes them look like they're zooming forward!
badges.fun_fact: The two chevrons come from V-shaped gear teeth. Citroën's founder, André Citroën, made these 'herringbone' gears before he ever built cars, so he used their shape as his logo!

badges.description: This shiny chrome badge looks like two pointy race-car shields stacked on top of each other, making a cool figure-8 shape! The inside sparkles with glittery white paint, like a little bit of starlight, and it may have been made to show off a powerful engine.
badges.fun_fact: Many cars use the number 8 on a badge to show they have a V8 engine, which has 8 cylinders working together like 8 tiny pumps to make the car go fast!

badges.description: This is a shiny metal nameplate that spells out RENAULT in big, chunky letters, the name of a famous French car maker! Each letter stands up tall like a little metal building, and they are all linked together by a thin bar. The worn, old-looking finish shows that this badge has been on a real adventure on a car driving down the road.
badges.fun_fact: Renault was started in France in 1899 by three brothers named Louis, Marcel and Fernand Renault, making it one of the oldest car companies in the world!

badges.description: This shiny badge spells FIAT in tall silver letters on a deep black shield, wrapped in a thick chrome frame shaped like a rounded square. It's the modern Fiat logo, inspired by the classic badges Fiat used in the early 1900s. The black version gives it a sleek, sporty, after-dark look compared to the usual red one!
badges.fun_fact: FIAT stands for 'Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino,' which means 'Italian Automobile Factory of Turin.' The company started in Italy way back in 1899!

badges.years: Approx. 1970s-1980s (this tall lettering style; reproductions are still made today)
badges.badge_name: Wheel Center Cap / Center Cap Emblem
badges.description: This shiny black circle shows the name FIAT in tall, skinny silver letters that look like they're standing at attention! A badge like this sat in the middle of a car's wheel and spun round and round as the car zoomed down the road. Those tiny scratches mean it has probably been on some real adventures.
badges.fun_fact: FIAT stands for 'Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino,' which means 'Italian Automobile Factory of Turin.' The company started in Italy way back in 1899!

badges.description: This is the Peugeot lion, standing tall on its back legs as if it's ready to roar! It's made of shiny silver, with one half brushed like metal and the other half polished like a mirror, set on a glossy black circle. Peugeot put this lion on the middle of their wheels, so it spun around every time the car drove.
badges.fun_fact: Peugeot is a French company that made pepper grinders and saws before it ever built cars. It chose a lion as its logo to show that its steel saw blades were as strong and sharp as a lion's teeth!

badges.description: This shiny black shield shows a big silver lion's head with its mouth open in a mighty roar and its mane flowing back like it's racing in the wind! The name PEUGEOT is printed down the side in sleek silver letters. It's the newest version of the lion badge, so it came from a modern Peugeot built in the 2020s.
badges.fun_fact: Peugeot has used a lion as its symbol since 1850, before it even made cars! The lion first appeared on saw blades and other steel tools to show they were as strong and sharp as a lion's teeth.

badges.description: This is the famous Renault diamond, made of shiny chrome that looks like a chunky gem! The thick silver frame folds around a smaller diamond window in the middle, so it looks almost like a 3D puzzle. It sparkles when light hits it, just like a jewel on the front of a French car.
badges.fun_fact: Renault is a French car company started in 1899 by three brothers, and its diamond-shaped logo has been used since 1925!

badges.description: This is a shiny Fiat badge with a silver ring shaped like a wreath of leaves, like the crowns worn by winners in ancient times! Inside is a bright blue circle with the word FIAT in silver letters. It came from an Italian car built around the year 2000, like a Fiat Punto, Stilo, Seicento or Panda.
badges.fun_fact: FIAT stands for 'Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino', which means 'Italian Automobile Factory of Turin'. This wreath badge was introduced in 1999 to celebrate Fiat's 100th birthday and was inspired by a Fiat logo from the 1920s!

badges.description: This shiny chrome nameplate spells out CITROËN in big, chunky 3D letters, just like it looked on the back of a French car! Look closely at the E: it wears two little round dots on top, which is a special French spelling trick. Each letter has a beveled mirror edge that sparkles in the light.
badges.fun_fact: Citroën's famous double-chevron logo comes from a gear with V-shaped teeth that the company's founder, André Citroën, made before he started building cars!

badges.description: This shiny chrome diamond is the famous Renault 'Losange,' the badge of a French car maker! Its sides slope inward like the facets of a giant jewel, making a hollow diamond window in the middle. It would have sparkled on the front grille or back hatch of a Renault car.
badges.fun_fact: Renault started in 1899, when three French brothers named Louis, Marcel and Fernand Renault built their first car. The company has used a diamond-shaped badge since the 1920s!

badges.description: This shiny badge has the word FIAT in bold white letters on a deep blue circle, like a little blue ocean in the middle. Around it is a sparkly chrome ring shaped like a wreath of leaves, the kind given to winners long ago. It rode on Italian cars such as the Punto, Panda, Stilo, Seicento and Doblo.
badges.fun_fact: FIAT stands for 'Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino', which means 'Italian Car Factory of Turin'. This blue wreath badge was made for Fiat's 100th birthday in 1999 and was inspired by a Fiat logo from the 1920s!

badges.badge_name: Wheel Center Cap / Hub Emblem Insert
badges.description: This shiny badge shows the famous Fiat '500' logo. The 5 and the two zeros join together in one curvy silver outline, like a squiggly snake! Here it is turned sideways on a glossy black circle with a bright chrome ring, and it probably sat in the middle of a wheel on a tiny Italian city car.
badges.fun_fact: The new Fiat 500 was launched on July 4, 2007, exactly 50 years after the original little Fiat 500 launched on July 4, 1957. In Italy people call it the 'Cinquecento,' which means 'five hundred'!

badges.description: This is the famous Renault diamond, called the 'Losange' in French! Its shiny chrome sides slope inward like a sparkling gem and lead down to a dark diamond hole in the middle. It looks like a jewel that came off a French car!
badges.fun_fact: Renault has used a diamond-shaped logo since 1925. One story says the diamond was chosen because the car's horn sat behind the hood's front, and a diamond-shaped opening let the honk come through!

badges.description: This is the famous Alfa Romeo roundel, one of the oldest and fanciest car logos in the world! On one side is a red cross, the symbol of the city of Milan in Italy. On the other side is a giant green serpent wearing a crown and holding a person in its mouth. This badge has been on a real adventure, and you can see its cross has faded from bright red to a rusty orange.
badges.fun_fact: The crowned serpent is called the 'Biscione'. It came from the coat of arms of the Visconti family, who ruled Milan hundreds of years ago, long before cars were invented!

badges.description: This is the famous Škoda 'winged arrow' badge! A green arrow with a feathery wing zooms forward inside a shiny silver circle. Around it is a black ring with the name ŠKODA and a green leafy laurel branch, a symbol long used to stand for winning and victory.
badges.fun_fact: Škoda is one of the oldest car companies in the world. It started in 1895 in what is now the Czech Republic, and its very first products were bicycles, not cars!

badges.description: This is the famous BMW 'roundel', one of the most recognizable car logos in the world! It has shiny chrome letters B-M-W on a black ring, with a circle of blue and white checkered quarters in the middle. BMW stands for Bayerische Motoren Werke, which means Bavarian Motor Works in German.
badges.fun_fact: Lots of people think the blue and white logo is a spinning airplane propeller against a blue sky. That idea actually came from a BMW advertisement in 1929. The colors really come from the flag of Bavaria, the German state where BMW is from.

badges.years: Approx. 1997-2020 (classic black-ring roundel with chrome letters; this style is still sold as a replacement part)
badges.description: This is the famous BMW roundel! Shiny silver letters spell B-M-W on a glossy black ring, and in the middle is a circle cut into four slices of blue and white, like a checkerboard pizza. The thick chrome edge makes it sparkle on the back or front of the car.
badges.fun_fact: Lots of people think the blue-and-white center is a spinning airplane propeller, but it really comes from the blue-and-white colors of Bavaria, the part of Germany where BMW was born. The propeller story came from an old BMW ad in 1929!

badges.description: This shiny round badge comes from a car dealership called Euro Motorcars, not from a car factory! It has three bright stripes in red, blue, and yellow, wrapped by a gleaming chrome ring with the dealer's name. A dealership that sold European cars probably stuck it on the back of a car.
badges.fun_fact: Car dealerships sometimes put their own little badges on the cars they sell, so every car driving around town works like a tiny moving advertisement for the dealer!

badges.badge_name: BMW Roundel Emblem (hood or trunk badge)
badges.description: This is the famous BMW roundel, a round badge with a shiny black ring and silver B-M-W letters around the edge. In the middle, two blue and two white slices form a cool checkerboard circle. The peeling, cracked finish shows it spent years out in the sun, rain and snow on a real BMW!
badges.fun_fact: The blue and white in the BMW logo come from the flag of Bavaria, the part of Germany where BMW started. Many people think it shows a spinning airplane propeller, but that idea came from an old BMW advertisement made after the logo was created.

badges.years: Circa 1997-present (this classic roundel style is still used on BMW cars)
badges.description: This is the famous BMW roundel. It has shiny silver letters riding around a glossy black ring like a racetrack! In the middle, four blue and white pieces fit together like a checkerboard pie, split by a bright silver cross.
badges.fun_fact: BMW stands for 'Bayerische Motoren Werke,' which means Bavarian Motor Works in German, and the blue and white colors come from the flag of Bavaria, the part of Germany where BMW was born.

badges.description: This is the famous BMW roundel! It has a shiny black ring with silver letters spelling B-M-W, and a circle in the middle split into four pieces of blue and white like a checkerboard pie. You can find this badge on the hood, trunk and wheels of BMW cars all over the world.
badges.fun_fact: Lots of people think the BMW logo is a spinning airplane propeller, but the blue and white really come from the flag of Bavaria, the part of Germany where BMW started out building airplane engines!

badges.description: This is the famous BMW roundel! It has a shiny black ring with silver letters B-M-W and a circle split into four slices, like a pizza cut into quarters. The blue slices have been worn down by sun, rain and lots of miles, so you can see the silver metal shining through, which shows it really traveled on a car!
badges.fun_fact: Lots of people think the BMW logo is a spinning airplane propeller, but its blue and white colors actually come from the flag of Bavaria, the part of Germany where BMW was born. The propeller story came from an old 1929 advertisement!

badges.description: This shiny badge spells out 'xDrive', with a big sparkly chrome X crossing a glossy black bar full of silver letters. BMW put this name on cars that send power to all four wheels, so they can grip snowy, muddy or slippery roads. It looks like a superhero's sash for a tough BMW SUV!
badges.fun_fact: BMW's xDrive system can move power between the front and back wheels in a split second, faster than you can blink, to help keep the car from slipping.

badges.years: 1997-present (this roundel style has been used for decades)
badges.badge_name: BMW Roundel Emblem (likely Wheel Center Cap)
badges.description: This is the famous BMW roundel! It has a shiny black ring with silver B-M-W letters and a circle split into four slices of blue and white, like a checkerboard pie. BMW puts this badge on the hood, the trunk and the middle of the wheels of its cars.
badges.fun_fact: BMW stands for 'Bayerische Motoren Werke,' which means Bavarian Motor Works. The blue and white colors come from the flag of Bavaria, a part of Germany. Many people think the logo is a spinning airplane propeller, but that idea started with a BMW advertisement in 1929!

badges.description: This is the famous BMW roundel, one of the most recognizable car badges in the world! It has a shiny black ring with silver B-M-W letters, wrapped around a circle split into blue and white checker-style quarters. Badges like this have ridden on everything from speedy sports sedans to motorcycles.
badges.fun_fact: Lots of people think the blue and white BMW logo is a spinning airplane propeller, but it actually comes from the blue and white colors of Bavaria, the German state where BMW was born. The propeller story became popular from a BMW ad in 1929, and BMW really did start out building airplane engines!

badges.years: Roundel design in this style used roughly 1970s-2020s
badges.description: This is the famous BMW roundel, a black ring with shiny silver letters spelling B-M-W around a circle of blue and white checkered quarters. Badges like this have ridden on super-fast German sports sedans, coupes and motorcycles all over the world. The flat metal design means it was probably stuck onto a wheel cap or another part of the car.
badges.fun_fact: Lots of people think the BMW logo shows a spinning airplane propeller, but the blue and white really come from the flag of Bavaria, the part of Germany where BMW was born. BMW stands for 'Bayerische Motoren Werke', which means 'Bavarian Motor Works'!

badges.badge_name: BMW Roundel Emblem (likely hood or trunk badge)
badges.description: This is the famous BMW roundel, a shiny black ring with silver B-M-W letters wrapped around a circle of blue and white checker quarters. The blue and white come from the flag of Bavaria, the part of Germany where BMW was born. It is one of the most recognized car logos in the whole world!
badges.fun_fact: BMW stands for Bayerische Motoren Werke, which means Bavarian Motor Works in German, and the company started out building airplane engines before it ever made cars.

badges.description: This is the famous Mercedes-Benz three-pointed star, shining in chrome inside a perfect circle! It probably stood proudly on the front of the hood, sticking up like a gunsight so the driver could see it while driving. The little stub on the side is where it once connected to its springy base.
badges.fun_fact: The three points of the Mercedes star stand for making engines for land, sea and air. The hood star was also built on a spring, so it could fold over if something bumped it instead of breaking!

badges.description: This is the famous Mercedes-Benz three-pointed star, shining in chrome on a sparkly dotted silver background! Around it is a deep blue ring with a leafy laurel wreath and the words MERCEDES-BENZ, like a winner's crown. Badges like this sat on the front hood of fancy Mercedes cars like the C-Class and E-Class.
badges.fun_fact: The three points of the Mercedes star stand for land, sea and air, because the company wanted its engines to power cars, boats and airplanes! The laurel wreath comes from the Benz company's logo, which joined the star when Daimler and Benz merged in 1926.

badges.description: This cap shows the famous Mercedes three-pointed star, molded right into the cap so it pops up like a 3D sculpture! Along the side, the name 'MERCEDES' is stamped in raised letters, like a secret signature. It is all one cream color, so you can find the star by its shape and shadows.
badges.fun_fact: The three points of the Mercedes star stand for the company's dream of building engines for the land, the sea and the air!

badges.description: This is the famous Mercedes-Benz three-pointed star, standing up proudly in the middle of a shiny silver cap! It snapped into the center of a Mercedes alloy wheel, where it spun around and around as the car zoomed down the road. Old Mercedes cars like the boxy 190E and the big S-Class wore caps like this.
badges.fun_fact: The three points of the Mercedes star stand for making engines for land, sea, and air!

badges.years: Approximately 1990s-2020s (the three-pointed star in a ring has been used since 1916)
badges.description: This is the famous Mercedes-Benz three-pointed star, shining in bright chrome inside a perfect circle! Its three arms are shaped like sharp, shiny blades that meet right in the middle, and behind them is a cool frosty, sparkly background. It is one of the most famous car logos in the whole world!
badges.fun_fact: The three points of the Mercedes star stand for the company's dream of building engines for land, sea and air!

badges.description: This shiny silver plate spells out 'Mercedes-Benz' in fancy thin letters, the same style the company uses on its fanciest cars. It looks like the name tag that sits on genuine Mercedes floor mats or inside trim, so it was probably inside the car rather than on the outside!
badges.fun_fact: The name 'Mercedes' came from a little girl! Mercedes Jellinek was the 10-year-old daughter of a businessman who raced and sold the cars, and they were named after her in 1901.

badges.years: Hyundai has used this slanted-H oval logo since about 1990. This black-mesh, brushed-metal style looks aftermarket, so its exact years are unknown.
badges.description: This is the famous Hyundai logo, a shiny silver letter H that leans to the side as if it's zooming forward! It sits inside a smooth oval frame, and the black mesh behind it looks like a sporty race-car grille.
badges.fun_fact: The slanted H in Hyundai's logo is meant to look like two people shaking hands, a company person and a happy customer!

badges.description: This shiny chrome badge shows the famous VW logo: a V sitting on top of a W, locked inside a big silver circle. The letters stand out in 3D like a mini sculpture, with dark shadowy spaces around them that make the chrome sparkle even more. It was mounted on the front grille or the back of a Volkswagen like a Golf, Jetta, Passat or Beetle.
badges.fun_fact: Volkswagen means 'people's car' in German. The V stands for 'Volks' (people) and the W stands for 'Wagen' (car)!

badges.description: This shiny silver badge shows the famous Volkswagen logo, a big V sitting right on top of a W, all inside a circle! The black spaces make the silver letters pop out like a secret code. It probably sat in the middle of a VW wheel, spinning round and round as the car zoomed down the road.
badges.fun_fact: Volkswagen means 'people's car' in German, which is why the logo is made of a V and a W!

badges.years: 2006-2018 (likely; similar covers continued on later Sprinters)
badges.description: This is a big tough hub cap from a Mercedes-Benz Sprinter, a giant work van that carries packages, tools and even groups of people! Right in the middle is the famous Mercedes three-pointed star, molded right into the strong plastic. The six little pockets around the edge fit over the wheel's lug nuts, which hold the wheel onto the van.
badges.fun_fact: The three points of the Mercedes-Benz star stand for making engines for travel on land, on water and in the air!

badges.description: This shiny badge shows the famous Volkswagen logo, a big V stacked on top of a W, all inside a chrome circle! The bright silver letters pop out against the black background like a superhero symbol. Your photo has it turned sideways, so tilt your head to spot the V and the W!
badges.fun_fact: Volkswagen means 'people's car' in German. The company's Beetle became one of the best-selling cars ever, with more than 21 million built!

badges.description: This is the famous Volkswagen logo: a shiny chrome circle with a big V sitting on top of a W, like a puzzle that fits perfectly! It's shown upside down in the photo, so flip it over and the VW will pop out. The chrome letters stand up tall like a 3D sculpture, and the scratches and spots show it went on lots of road trips.
badges.fun_fact: Volkswagen means 'people's car' in German. The V stands for 'Volks' (people) and the W stands for 'Wagen' (car)!

badges.years: Approx. 2000-2019 (pre-2019 VW logo style; many aftermarket versions)
badges.description: This is the famous Volkswagen logo: a big 'V' stacked on top of a 'W' inside a circle. The shiny brushed-metal letters sit on a deep black background under a clear bubble dome that makes it sparkle. Badges like this ride in the middle of a VW's wheels and spin around super fast when the car drives!
badges.fun_fact: Volkswagen means 'people's car' in German, and the VW Beetle became one of the best-selling cars in history, with over 21 million built!

badges.description: This shiny chrome badge shows the famous Volkswagen logo, a 'V' sitting on top of a 'W' inside a circle! The letters pop up like a 3D sculpture, and the dark spaces between them make the chrome really stand out. It's turned sideways in the picture, so spin it around and you'll see the VW clearly!
badges.fun_fact: Volkswagen means 'people's car' in German, and the VW Beetle became one of the best-selling cars in history, with more than 21 million made!

badges.description: This shiny chrome circle holds the famous VW letters, with a pointy V stacked on top of a zig-zag W. The letters are cut out so you can see right through them, a style that used to sit proudly on the front grilles of Volkswagens. All those scratches show it rode down a lot of real roads!
badges.fun_fact: The name Volkswagen means 'people's car' in German, which is why the logo uses a V and a W.

badges.description: This is the famous Peugeot lion, standing up tall on its back legs like it's ready to pounce! It has sharp claws, a roaring mouth and a curly tail with a pointy tip. It's all shiny chrome, so it sparkled on the front or back of a French car.
badges.fun_fact: Peugeot started out making pepper grinders, saws and bicycles before it made cars. The lion logo was chosen to show its steel saw blades were as strong and sharp as a lion's teeth!

badges.description: This shiny round badge has a gold FIAT logo tucked inside a rounded shield, glowing on a deep black background like treasure in a dark cave! The chrome ring around the edge made it sparkle on a little Italian car from long ago. The cool 'A' with no line across the middle was a special design trick Fiat used back in the swinging '60s!
badges.fun_fact: FIAT stands for 'Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino,' which means 'Italian Automobile Factory of Turin.' The company started way back in 1899!

badges.badge_name: Wheel Center Cap / Alloy Wheel Emblem
badges.description: This is the famous Opel 'Blitz' logo: a shiny chrome lightning bolt zapping right through a silver ring! It sat in the middle of an alloy wheel on an Opel car from Germany, spinning around super fast every time the car drove. Notice how the bolt breaks out of the circle at the top and bottom, like electricity escaping!
badges.fun_fact: 'Blitz' is the German word for lightning, and Opel's lightning bolt logo came from its speedy truck called the Opel Blitz. Before Opel ever built cars, the company made sewing machines and bicycles!

badges.description: This shiny chrome badge uses a cool, sporty secret code instead of letters! The slanted stripes and pointy notches make it look like it's zooming forward even when the car is parked. It's a modern-style logo that Mercury cars wore back in the 1980s and 1990s.
badges.fun_fact: Mercury was named after the speedy Roman messenger god with wings on his helmet, and Ford stopped making Mercury cars in 2011, so every Mercury badge is now a piece of history!

badges.badge_name: Wheel Center Cap Emblem Insert (flat logo disc)
badges.description: This is the famous Volkswagen logo, a big V sitting on top of a W inside a circle, in shiny silver and black! It's been on some real adventures, with dents and scratches that show it rode around on a car for many miles. Turn it sideways and you'll see the V and W pop right out!
badges.fun_fact: Volkswagen means 'people's car' in German, and the V and W in the logo stand for those two words!

badges.description: This shiny badge shows Volkswagen's famous logo: a V stacked on top of a W inside a circle. The silver letters pop up off a black background covered in tiny dots, like a mini racetrack grip pattern! Turn it the right way and you'll see the classic VW that rides on Beetles, Golfs and Jettas all over the world.
badges.fun_fact: Volkswagen means 'people's car' in German. The V stands for 'Volks' (people) and the W stands for 'Wagen' (car)!

badges.description: This is the famous Volkswagen logo, with a big shiny V sitting on top of a W inside a chrome circle! The black background has tiny dots like a mini golf ball, which makes the silver letters really pop. This puffy, 3D-looking chrome style was used on many VWs from about 2000 until the late 2010s.
badges.fun_fact: Volkswagen means 'people's car' in German, and the V and W in the logo stand for those two words!

badges.description: This shiny cap sat in the middle of an Audi wheel and spun around super fast every time the car drove down the road! It shows Audi's famous four silver rings linked together like a chain on a cool metallic grey background. The bright chrome edge makes it sparkle like a medal.
badges.fun_fact: Audi's four rings stand for four car companies, Audi, DKW, Horch and Wanderer, that joined together in 1932 to make one big team called Auto Union!

badges.years: Approx. 1995-2022 (3D chrome four-ring style; Audi moved to flat 2D rings around 2022)
badges.badge_name: Four Rings Emblem (grille or trunk badge)
badges.description: This is the famous Audi badge: four shiny silver rings linked together like a chain! The chrome rings sparkle like mirrors and stick out in 3D, so they really shine on the front grille or the back of an Audi. It looks a bit like part of the Olympic rings, but it is all Audi!
badges.fun_fact: The four rings stand for four German car companies, Audi, DKW, Horch and Wanderer, which joined together in 1932 to make one team called Auto Union.

badges.years: Four-ring logo used since 1932 (Auto Union) and by Audi since 1985; this glitter-filled style is a modern aftermarket piece, likely 2000s-2020s
badges.description: This is the famous Audi badge: four shiny chrome rings linked together like a chain! This one is extra fancy because the inside of each ring is packed with sparkly silver glitter, so it twinkles like treasure when light hits it.
badges.fun_fact: The four rings stand for four German car companies (Audi, DKW, Horch and Wanderer) that joined together in 1932 to make one big team called Auto Union.

badges.years: Likely 1960s-1980s (based on the chrome die-cast style)
badges.description: This shiny silver badge is made of chunky metal numbers with super-sharp pointy corners, like little chrome swords! Badges like this were stuck on the side or back of a car to show its model number or how big its engine was. It's a cool mystery piece, because no brand name is shown, so it's like a puzzle waiting to be solved!
badges.fun_fact: Many cars wore number badges to brag about their engines. A '1600' badge often meant a 1.6-liter engine, which is about the size of a big bottle of soda!
